cases.title: The Family and Witnesses Who Didn't Follow Brigham
cases.claim: When Joseph Smith was killed in June 1844, he left no unambiguous succession plan, and the movement fractured among rival claimants: counselor Sidney Rigdon, the Quorum of the Twelve under Brigham Young, and James Strang — who produced a letter of appointment dated June 1844 (now at Yale's Beinecke Library, catalogued as 'attributed'), then unearthed his own metal plates at Voree, Wisconsin in 1845 before four witnesses, and there is no direct contemporaneous evidence his witnesses ever recanted (a fact that complicates appeals to the Book of Mormon witnesses). Strikingly, the people who knew Joseph best did not go west. His widow Emma stayed in Nauvoo, married the non-Mormon Lewis Bidamon, and in her 1879 'Last Testimony' (Saints' Herald, Oct. 1, 1879) denied to her death that Joseph practiced polygamy: 'He had no other wife but me.' His mother Lucy and brother William never gathered to Utah; his son Joseph Smith III became prophet of the rival RLDS church at Amboy, Illinois in 1860. None of the Three Witnesses went west in 1847: all were excommunicated by 1838; Oliver Cowdery was rebaptized in 1848 but died before reaching Utah; Martin Harris came only in 1870; David Whitmer never returned.

sources.name: Joseph Smith (attributed), 'Letter of Appointment,' June 18, 1844 — Beinecke Library, Yale
Emma Smith, 'Last Testimony of Sister Emma' (1879) — B. H. Roberts source archive
Joseph Smith Papers — Emma Hale Smith biography
BYU Religious Studies Center — 'Six Days in August: Brigham Young and the Succession Crisis of 1844'
Literary Hub — 'The Forged Letter That Began a Mormon Succession Crisis'

cases.response: LDS apologists answer that succession did not depend on family: Joseph conferred the keys of the kingdom on the Quorum of the Twelve before his death, and the great majority of Nauvoo Saints sustained the Twelve over Rigdon on August 8, 1844. Strang's letter of appointment is judged a forgery on handwriting and postal grounds, and apologists contend several Voree witnesses later distanced themselves from Strang. As for Emma, FAIR argues her denials are contradicted by overwhelming documentary evidence — including sealing records naming her participation in 1843 — and are explained by her desire to protect her sons, her opposition to polygamy, her property disputes with Brigham Young, and loyalty to the RLDS movement her son led. Family proximity, they note, is not the biblical test of truth.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Emma Smith and Brigham Young

cases.rationale: Every constituent fact is conceded on all sides: no written succession plan was ever produced, Emma and the Smith family rejected Brigham Young, Joseph Smith III led the rival RLDS church, and Emma denied polygamy until death. What remains contested is the meaning. The keys-to-the-Twelve argument has genuine historical support, and the majority of Nauvoo Saints did follow the Twelve — so the case cannot be graded as unrefuted. But the defense carries a heavy cost the apologists rarely name: it requires asserting that the prophet's own widow lied publicly and consistently for thirty-five years, while simultaneously treating friendly witnesses as unimpeachable. And the standard LDS dismissal of Strang's plates and never-fully-recanting witnesses applies with uncomfortable symmetry to the Book of Mormon's own witness apparatus.

cases.title: The Second Anointing: A Secret Ordinance Above the Endowment
cases.claim: Beyond the endowment sits a higher ordinance most Latter-day Saints have never heard of: the second anointing, in which a couple's 'calling and election is made sure' and exaltation is sealed upon them (cf. D&C 131:5, 'the more sure word of prophecy'). It has been administered since September 28, 1843, by invitation of the First Presidency only. David John Buerger's landmark study in Dialogue (1983) documents thousands performed in the nineteenth century, then a sharp curtailment and near-total concealment in the twentieth — the church stopped publishing statistics by the 1930s, and even the LDS-apologetic site Mormonr confirms the ordinance exists, is invitation-only, 'isn't generally taught in Church meetings or in Church publications,' and that teachers are instructed not to discuss or answer questions about it. It came to broad public light in 2012 when Tom Phillips, a former stake president who received the rite from apostle M. Russell Ballard, published a detailed firsthand account and told his story on Mormon Stories. Scripture offers assurance of salvation freely to every believer (1 John 5:13; Romans 8:16) — not as a secret rite reserved for elites.

sources.name: David John Buerger, '"The Fulness of the Priesthood": The Second Anointing in Latter-day Saint Theology and Practice,' Dialogue 16:1 (1983)
Tom Phillips, 'My Second Anointing Experience' (firsthand account)
Mormon Stories — Tom Phillips and the Second Anointing (2012 interview)

cases.response: LDS defenders do not deny the ordinance exists; they defend its privacy. Mormonr frames the second anointing as sacred rather than secret — treated with the same reticence as other temple matters, not a conspiracy. They note biblical precedent for anointing individuals (priests and kings were anointed; Jesus spoke of mysteries given to some and not others), and stress that the ordinance is conditional, not an unconditional guarantee of exaltation, so it does not bypass the need for enduring faithfulness. The rarity, they argue, reflects prudence about a blessing that could be misunderstood, and ordinary members lose nothing: the same blessings are held out to all the faithful, and ordinances not received in this life may be received hereafter. Silence protects sacredness, not a hierarchy of salvation.
cases.rationale: This is graded admitted because the apologetic side itself confirms every factual element of the claim: the ordinance exists, is administered by invitation of the church's highest leadership, is absent from public teaching, and members are explicitly instructed not to discuss it. The only dispute is characterization — 'sacred' versus 'secret' — and whether a conditional sealing differs meaningfully from a guaranteed one. The evangelistic force is untouched by that framing: a two-tier system in which an inner circle receives a hidden assurance ordinary members do not know exists stands in stark contrast to the New Testament, where assurance is proclaimed openly and offered to all believers on the basis of faith in Christ, and where 2 Peter 1:10 addresses every reader of a public epistle, not initiates of a private rite.

cases.title: Joseph's Corrected Bible — Which His Church Never Adopted
cases.claim: From June 1830 to July 1833, Joseph Smith produced an 'inspired revision' of the entire Bible, altering roughly 3,400 verses with no manuscript support — and declared it done: 'We this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' (History of the Church, July 2, 1833). Revelations had commanded the work be finished (D&C 73:4) and published (D&C 124:89). Yet the LDS church has never adopted it. Its official Bible remains the King James Version, with selected JST readings relegated to footnotes and an appendix; it was the rival RLDS church (Community of Christ) that published the full text as the Inspired Version in 1867 and held the manuscripts for 150 years — until the LDS church bought them, along with the marked Bible and the Kirtland Temple, in the $192.5 million deal of March 2024. Stranger still, BYU's own scholars concede the 1830 Book of Mormon was used as a source for some JST changes to Isaiah, while many Book of Mormon–KJV variants were never carried into the JST at all and some were changed yet again — meaning Joseph revised verses his own earlier scripture quotes in their KJV form. If God commissioned a corrected Bible, why doesn't the restored church use it?

sources.name: BYU Studies — 'The Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible' (Robert J. Matthews)
Church History Topics — 'Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible'
Deseret News — 'What the LDS Church received from Community of Christ' (March 2024)
Church Newsroom — FAQ on the transfer of sacred sites and historic documents (2024)
Mormonism Research Ministry (evangelical) — 'The Inspired Version: Why Isn't It Officially Used Today?'

cases.response: FAIR and BYU scholars respond that the July 1833 'finished' statement marked the end of the first pass, not a canon-ready text: Joseph continued revising until his death in 1844, never prepared a final publication manuscript, and D&C 124:89's command to publish went unfulfilled amid poverty and persecution — so the church inherited an unfinished working draft, not a completed Bible. They add that the JST was never meant as a uniform restoration of original text; it blends textual restoration, prophetic commentary, harmonization, and modernization, which explains divergences from Book of Mormon readings without contradiction. Far from suppressing it, the church incorporated hundreds of JST readings into its 1979 KJV edition's footnotes and appendix, and the 2024 acquisition of the manuscripts reflects reverence for the work, not embarrassment about it.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Joseph's Translation of the Bible (response to MormonThink)

cases.rationale: The core facts are undisputed: the revision was commanded, pronounced finished in Joseph's own record in 1833, commanded to be published in 1841, never canonized by the LDS church, and published instead by the rival denomination that rejected Brigham Young. The apologetic reply — that it was actually unfinished and multi-genre — is a genuine scholarly position (Joseph did keep tinkering), which keeps this contested rather than unrefuted. But the defense sits awkwardly with the primary sources: it must read 'we this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' as not meaning finished, and it concedes the revelation commanding publication was never obeyed. And the category problem remains on any reading: a prophet corrected the Bible by revelation, and the church claiming his mantle still hands members the uncorrected KJV.

didyouknow.t: The Word of Wisdom's forgotten beer clause
didyouknow.d: D&C 89:17 designates barley 'for mild drinks' — a phrase early Saints understood to permit beer, and the church's own history essay concedes that for two generations leaders tolerated milder alcoholic drinks, denouncing only whiskey and drunkenness. Total abstention became a temple-recommend requirement only under Heber J. Grant in the early 1920s, in step with the American temperance movement.

A silver Jupiter talisman — a magical astrological charm — was reportedly on Joseph Smith's person at Carthage, a claim popularized by D. Michael Quinn's Early Mormonism and the Magic World View. Honesty requires the caveat: the provenance rests entirely on an affidavit Charles Bidamon (son of Emma's second husband) gave when selling it in the 1930s, the talisman appears nowhere in the 1844 inventory of Joseph's effects, and the researcher who first presented it, Reed Durham, later retracted his claim of primary evidence.

didyouknow.t: The temple ceremony quietly changed in 2019
didyouknow.d: In January 2019 the endowment was revised so women no longer covenant to 'hearken' to their husbands — following a 1990 change that removed their promise to 'obey.' The First Presidency confirmed adjustments had been made without detailing them and asked members not to discuss specifics. Further documented revisions followed in 2023, part of a long pattern of changes to a ceremony presented as restored eternal ordinances.

didyouknow.t: One president announced more temples than 188 years of history built
didyouknow.d: President Russell M. Nelson announced 200 new temples in under eight years — more than the roughly 160 the church had managed to complete in its entire history before him. As of mid-2026 the church counts 385 temples total, but only 219 are dedicated (211 operating); 61 are under construction and 105 remain merely announced, many still without sites or groundbreaking dates.
